passage:
Note, Class 5, week 3. Uday's hand shoots up before I finish reading a question. On Monday I asked, "What is 7 plus 8, minus 5?" and Uday called "15" at once. The answer was 10. His face fell and he looked at his desk. At break I sat with him and offered a small trick: count silently to three, then read the question again. On Wednesday he raised his hand after a long breath and answered a fraction question correctly. By Friday he glanced at the question card twice each time. I praised the checking, not the speed.

Minakshi, class teacher

qa.q: What answer did Uday call out on Monday?
How did Uday feel after the wrong answer?
qa.a: Uday felt embarrassed and disappointed, since his face fell and he looked at his desk.

qa.q: What else could Uday do to avoid blurting out?
qa.a: Uday could jot the answer on a scrap of paper first, or wait until the teacher says a name.

qa.q: How might a classmate see Uday's new pause?
qa.a: A classmate may see Uday as more careful, and may feel there is a fair chance to answer too.

grounding: Shows a boy who blurted a wrong answer learning to count to three and re-read the question before answering.

passage:
Thursday

Today in maths Miss Elizabeth asked, "What is half of 18?" and I shouted "Six!" before she even finished. Everyone laughed. It was nine. I knew it was nine. My face went hot. Afterwards Miss Elizabeth said to me, "Akash, you're quick, but try this: count one, two, three in your head, and read the question again." In English I tried it. She asked how many syllables "butterfly" has. I wanted to shout "two!" I counted one, two, three, said it in my head, but-ter-fly, and said "Three." She smiled. "Good thinking, young man." I'm going to do it tomorrow too. It feels slow but it's better than everyone laughing.

qa.q: What did Akash shout when asked half of 18?
How did Akash feel when everyone laughed?
qa.a: Akash felt embarrassed and hot in the face, especially because the right answer was known.

qa.q: What else could help Akash when he feels the urge to shout?
qa.a: Put a hand up first and take a breath while counting, so there's time to check the question.

qa.q: How might Miss Elizabeth see the change in English?
qa.a: Miss Elizabeth seems pleased and proud, smiling when the pause leads to the right answer.

grounding: After blurting a wrong answer, a boy learns to count to three and check the question before he answers in class.

passage: In the village school near Sangli, Farhan was known for his hand shooting up first. On Monday the teacher asked, "Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of stones?" "Stones!" Farhan shouted. The class burst out laughing. His friend Samir whispered, "Both are a kilo, yaar." Farhan's ears burned. That evening, walking home past the sugarcane fields, he said, "I'm going to count to three before I answer. Every time." Samir grinned. "Bet you can't." On Tuesday the teacher asked how many legs a spider has. Farhan's hand went up, but his lips moved: one, two, three. He read the question on the board again. "Eight," he said. Samir gave him a thumbs up under the desk.

qa.q: What question did Farhan get wrong on Monday?
qa.a: Which is heavier, a kilo of cotton or a kilo of stones.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed; his ears burned.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to help children like Farhan?
qa.a: Give a few seconds of thinking time before calling on anyone, so pausing becomes normal for the whole class.

qa.q: How does Samir see Farhan's new habit?
qa.a: Samir teases him at first but is pleased and supportive when it works, giving a thumbs up.

grounding: After blurting a wrong answer, a boy learns to count to three and reread the question before answering in class.
